test_title: RRB Group D Previous Year Paper (Held on: 15 Sept 2022 Shift 3)
subject: general
question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about voluntary muscles?

options.text: Cells are long, cylindrical, unbranched and uninucleate.
These muscles are also called skeletal muscles.
These muscles show alternate light and dark bands.
They are mostly attached to bones.

solution:
The correct answer is __**1) Cells are long, cylindrical, unbranched and uninucleate.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Voluntary muscles are also known as skeletal muscles because they are usually attached to bones and can be consciously controlled.
 
• These muscles are characterized by their striated appearance, showing alternate light and dark bands.
 
• Cells of voluntary muscles are long, cylindrical, and typically multinucleate, not uninucleate.
 
• These muscles play a crucial role in movements and locomotion of the body.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Voluntary Muscles**

 
 
• These muscles are under conscious control, meaning they can be voluntarily moved.
 
• Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tendons and are responsible for movement.
 
• The structure of these muscles includes muscle fibers that are long and cylindrical, containing multiple nuclei (multinucleate).
 
• The striated appearance of these muscles is due to the arrangement of actin and myosin filaments within the muscle cells.
 
 
 
• **Involuntary Muscles**
 
 
• These muscles are not under conscious control and function automatically.
 
• Examples include smooth muscles found in the walls of internal organs and blood vessels, and cardiac muscles found in the heart.
 
• Smooth muscles are spindle-shaped, unstriated, and uninucleate.
 
• Cardiac muscles are striated like skeletal muscles but are branched and typically uninucleate.
